style_when: the article explains how a system, process or stack actually works — money flows, supply chains, pipelines, an agent assembly line
prompt: Clean technical isometric cutaway of a warehouse aisle, split-screen diptych: left half shows two different unbranded robot fleets at a crossing aisle exchanging a small printed ISO document page with blank fields, right half shows an Amazon-style modular storage rack with a meter face marked by a blank percentage wedge. Single hard key light rakes from upper left across brushed steel robot housings and concrete floor; palette graphite, safety yellow, bone white; thin consistent line weight, matte surfaces, no text, no numbers.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, legible numbers, UI text, blurry, low contrast
rationale: The story turns on a published standard and a fee notice, not a photographable single scene; technical_isometric can diagram both costs as physical mechanisms inside one warehouse, with split-screen contrasting the lock-breaking exit route against the growing rental surcharge.
subject: a modular warehouse bay with two robot fleets exchanging a printed standard document at a crossing aisle and a rental surcharge meter on the opposite side
core_thesis: The automation payback model's two assumed costs—vendor exit and rented capacity—became public facts with opposite implications: a $373 ISO standard breaks vendor lock, while Amazon's 3.5% surcharge widens the rental cost.
core_conflict: Ownership lock-in versus rental exposure; exit cost turns out low via an open standard, while rental cost turns out variable and rising.
composition: split-screen diptych with left-right scenario contrast, extreme asymmetry, technical isometric view

review.depicts: An isometric split view showing, on the left, four robots on a concrete warehouse floor at a crossing aisle — two low bin-carrying mobile units and two tall arm-mounted units whose grippers hold up a blank white document sheet — and on the right, a tall steel shelving rack stacked with plastic bins and cartons, its end frame carrying a large plain metal panel bearing an unmarked shape.
review.reason: The left panel literally stages the article's core object — robot fleets exchanging a printed interoperability standard at a shared aisle — though the right panel shows generic racking rather than the promised rental-surcharge meter, so the second cost the headline rests on is not visible.
